text: CSF (Classical Swine Fever) is caused by a virus affecting only swine; antibiotics cannot treat it. Large amounts of virus concentrate in the tonsils and are shed via mouth, nose, and eyes. CSF is often under-diagnosed because PRRS gets more attention and can look similar on rough examination — careful clinical exam and necropsy lesions are needed to tell them apart, and highly pathogenic PRRS cases are actually often a CSF+PRRS combination. Virulence (how fast the virus multiplies) varies, giving acute disease (rapid death) to sub-acute disease (pigs usually survive but stay weak and grow slowly). Transmission: direct contact (mouth-to-mouth), via semen during mating, trans-placental infection of fetuses during pregnancy, feeding inadequately cooked garbage containing infected pork/organs, and people/equipment carrying the virus on shoes and clothes between farms. Symptoms usually appear 5–10 days after exposure; a hallmark sign is persistent high fever (>41°C) unresponsive to antibiotics, and pigs can shed virus before showing any symptoms. Acute disease (often in 30–60 kg fattening pigs): high fever, depression/weakness, conjunctivitis, incoordination, purple skin discoloration, sometimes green profuse diarrhea (secondary Salmonella) and respiratory signs, with high mortality within 1–2 weeks. Sub-acute disease (from low-virulence strains, poor-quality vaccine, broken cold chain, inadequate vaccination program, or wrong injection technique): fever may be the only sign, but persistent fever unresponsive to antibiotics should suggest CSF; small skin hemorrhages; huddling, inactivity, reduced appetite; secondary Salmonella/Pasteurella infection often follows, causing green profuse diarrhea and/or serious coughing and breathing difficulty. In sows: stillborn piglets, mummification, abortion, and weak/small live piglets — a distinguishing sign versus PRRS is newborn piglets trembling right after birth. Necropsy findings: dark red infarcts along the spleen margins, petechiae (pinpoint spots) in the lungs, hemorrhages in lymph nodes. Treatment: none directly (viral), and once CSF is confirmed, treating fattening pigs isn't recommended, since even 10 days of antibiotics won't restore normal growth and it becomes a financial loss; for gilts/young boars/sows worth saving, treatment focuses on lowering fever to restore appetite (Paracetamol), preventing secondary infection (Florfenicol, Doxycycline for green watery diarrhea, Tylosin+Gentamycin, or Enrofloxacin as a last resort), and supporting immunity with vitamins/stimulants. Prevention: proper vaccination is essential — arguably the single most important vaccine for any pig farm, small or large — using proven products from established manufacturers (e.g. Ceva, Intervet, Hipra); example program: piglets at 3 weeks (only needed if sows aren't regularly vaccinated), 7 weeks, and 11 weeks; sows vaccinated 1 month before farrowing to boost milk antibodies; gilts re-vaccinated at 6 months (with a second dose at 7 months if bought from an unknown vaccination history); boars vaccinated every 6 months.
